limn

A Projection Engine for Distributional Forecasting.

Prediction and forecasting for models fitted by illume: predictive distributions, forecasts, proper scoring rules, calibration, cross-validation and model comparison.

limn is the third package in a family, after illumex for exploration and illume for inference. All three use the ilm_ prefix, so one prefix finds a function in any of them. library(limn) attaches illume, which attaches illumex.

Status: early development

limn is pre-release: this is a development version, published before its first CRAN release. Its core is built and validated, and its interfaces may still change before then. The validation studies and their findings, with the prototypes behind some of its defaults, are in studies.

What exists now:

  • Prediction and forecasting:
    • ilm_predict(): the prediction engine. It gives the predictive distribution of the mean, a new observation or the linear predictor for new rows, with the fit’s own uncertainty. How the random effects enter is always named.
    • ilm_forecast(): forecasts past a series’ last observed time. A correlation over time (ilm_ar1(), ilm_car1(), ilm_rw1()) is carried forward from the fit’s own parameters, with no refit, as one path per draw.
    • ilm_future(): the rows a forecast needs, the next time points of every series, with time-varying covariates left for you to fill in.
    • ilm_covariate_paths() and ilm_as_draws(): covariates whose future is uncertain, given as draws, so the forecast mixes over them. The draws are simulated from an illume model of the covariate, or taken from elsewhere.
  • Totals and averages:
    • ilm_aggregate(): totals or averages over a series’ horizon, over every series at each time, or over all rows. They are taken draw by draw, so a path’s correlation carries into them.
    • ilm_average(): weighted averages of predicted means, for standardisation or post-stratification (as in MRP).
  • Evaluation:
    • ilm_scores() on a prediction, as a method of illume’s generic. It gives the log score, the CRPS, and the Brier, pinball, interval, squared and absolute scores. MASE and RMSSE take their scale from the training data or from ilm_naive_scale().
    • ilm_pit() and ilm_plot_pit(): probability integral transforms, randomised for discrete outcomes, and their histogram.
    • ilm_folds(): cross-validation folds that follow the data’s structure, with random, grouped, blocked and rolling-origin folds.
    • ilm_cv(): a model refitted to each fold, then scored on the rows it wasn’t fitted to.
    • ilm_compare(): two models’ scores compared, with standard errors clustered by group or fold, or Diebold-Mariano over forecast origins.
    • ilm_calibration() on a prediction, as a method of illume’s generic: coverage, bias, and a binary outcome’s calibration intercept and slope, with a verdict that names a remedy.
  • Diagnostic plots:
    • ilm_plot_fan(): a fan chart of predictive distributions over time;
    • ilm_plot_horizon(): scores by forecast horizon;
    • ilm_plot_compare(): comparisons with their intervals;
    • ilm_plot_calibration(): coverage, or reliability for a binary outcome.

Principles

  • A prediction is a distribution. It is a mixture over draws of the fitted parameters, so its intervals carry the fit’s own uncertainty. Every score is computed from that mixture, not from responses simulated from it.
  • How the random effects enter is always named. The choices are a unit seen in the fit, a new unit, a typical unit, or the population average. These answer different questions, and there is no default that suits every one.
  • Evaluation follows the data’s structure. Grouped folds score predictions for new units, and rolling origins score forecasts. Comparisons carry standard errors clustered the same way.
  • Every validity claim is measured against an independent implementation where one exists, and by simulation otherwise. The scripts are in studies/.

Installation

limn and the two packages it builds on are installed from GitHub:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("huttoncp/illumex")
remotes::install_github("huttoncp/illume")
remotes::install_github("huttoncp/limn")

How this package was built

limn’s code was written at Craig P. Hutton’s direction by his Claude Code sessions. Craig sets the design and approves every change that reaches the main branch.

What the model did. It prototyped and measured the design, and drafted the implementation, the documentation and the validation studies. It proposed designs, and argued for them when it thought a choice was wrong.

What the author did. Specified what the package should be and what it should refuse to do. Set the standing constraints:

  • illume’s exported interface only;
  • no benchmark methods inside the package;
  • no claim without a measurement behind it.

Made the decisions the design turned on: the shared prefix, that the user names how random effects enter a prediction, and which parts are built in limn and which in illume. Directs the order of the work.

Status of independent review. The author reviews the package and tests it independently of the development process. That work is in progress, and this paragraph will say when it is complete. Until then the package is pre-release, and should be treated as such.

The disclosure matters less than it might seem. The question about a statistical package is whether its claims are checkable and whether anyone checked them. limn’s answer is the same as illume’s: each validity claim is a comparison against an independent implementation that somebody else wrote, or a simulation study. The scripts and their findings are in studies/.

Acknowledgements

limn’s results are checked against three packages written by others: sandwich for clustered standard errors (Zeileis, Köll and Graham 2020) and a Newey-West long-run variance (Zeileis 2004), in the tests; scoringRules for the CRPS and the log score (Jordan, Krüger and Lerch 2019), in the tests and studies; and forecast for the Diebold-Mariano test (Hyndman and Khandakar 2008), in the studies. They are comparators: limn shares their methods, not their code.

  • Hyndman, R. J. and Khandakar, Y. (2008). Automatic time series forecasting: the forecast package for R. Journal of Statistical Software 27(3), 1-22. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v027.i03
  • Jordan, A., Krüger, F. and Lerch, S. (2019). Evaluating probabilistic forecasts with scoringRules. Journal of Statistical Software 90(12), 1-37. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v090.i12
  • Zeileis, A. (2004). Econometric computing with HC and HAC covariance matrix estimators. Journal of Statistical Software 11(10), 1-17. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v011.i10
  • Zeileis, A., Köll, S. and Graham, N. (2020). Various versatile variances: an object-oriented implementation of clustered covariances in R. Journal of Statistical Software 95(1), 1-36. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v095.i01
